step.markdown:
The derivatives of sine, cosine, and tangent are shown in the table below:

| $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ |
| --- | --- |
| $\sin x$ | $\cos x$ |
| $\cos x$ | $-\sin x$ |
| $\tan x$ | $\sec^2 x$ |

Now that we know the derivatives of the standard trigonometric functions, we can differentiate any combination of them by using the properties of differentiation.

For example, let's find the derivative of $y = \cos x + \sin x.$

Here, we can use the fact that the derivative of the sum is equal to the sum of the derivatives, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** We'll derive the derivatives shown in the table at the end of this lesson.

step.markdown: Find the derivative of $y =  3\cos x  + 4\sin x + 2x^3.$
step.solution:
We know that $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} ( \sin x ) = \cos x,$ and that $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} ( \cos x ) = -\sin x.$ Applying these formulas, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3cos⁡x+4sin⁡x+2{x}^{3}) \\  & =3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(cos⁡x)+4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(sin⁡x)+2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}) \\  & =-3sin⁡x+4cos⁡x+2(3){x}^{2} \\  & =-3sin⁡x+4cos⁡x+6{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

step.markdown:
Suppose that we have the two functions $u(x)=2x^3$ and $v(x)=x^2.$ How do we calculate the derivative of their product $(u(x) \cdot v(x))'?$

To do that, we can use the **product rule**, which states that the derivative of the product of two functions is given by the formula

$$
\left(u(x) \cdot  v(x)\right)' = u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x).
$$

In our case, the derivatives of the two functions are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(x) & =(2{x}^{3})^{′}=6{x}^{2}, \\ {v}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{2})^{′}=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

If we plug all of this into the product rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u(x)\cdot v(x))}^{′} & =(6{x}^{2})({x}^{2})+(2{x}^{3})(2x) \\  & =6{x}^{4}+4{x}^{4} \\  & =10{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

This example was quite simple, and we could have solved it by calculating the product first and then taking the derivative. We can do it now to double check our result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u(x)\cdot v(x))}^{′} & =(2{x}^{3}\cdot {x}^{2})^{′} \\  & =(2{x}^{5})^{′} \\  & =10{x}^{4}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Sometimes, however, we cannot calculate the product algebraically, or it can be tedious to do it. In those cases, the product rule will turn out to be very useful!

step.solution:
Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)=x$ and $v(x)=\cos x .$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
	 (x\cos x)' &=   u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x)\\
						&= (x)'\cdot \cos x + x\cdot (\cos x)'\\
					   & = 1 \cdot \cos x + x (-\sin x)\\
					  & =  \cos x - x \sin x					

\end{aligned}
$$

step.solution:
Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)=4 - x^{2}$ and $v(x)=\tan{\left(x \right)}.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}((4 - x^{2})(\tan{\left(x \right)}))^{'} & =u'(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot v'(x) \\ & =(4 - x^{2})'\cdot (\tan{\left(x \right)})+(4 - x^{2})\cdot (\tan{\left(x \right)})' \\ & =(- 2 x)(\tan{\left(x \right)})+(4 - x^{2})(\tan^{2}{\left(x \right)} + 1) \\ & =- x^{2} \tan^{2}{\left(x \right)} - x^{2} - 2 x \tan{\left(x \right)} + 4 \tan^{2}{\left(x \right)} + 4\end{aligned}
$$

step.solution:
Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)=4 x^{4} + x$ and $v(x)=\tan{\left(x \right)} + 2.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}((4 x^{4} + x)(\tan{\left(x \right)} + 2))^{'} & =u'(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot v'(x) \\ & =(4 x^{4} + x)'\cdot (\tan{\left(x \right)} + 2)+(4 x^{4} + x)\cdot (\tan{\left(x \right)} + 2)' \\ & =(16 x^{3} + 1)(\tan{\left(x \right)} + 2)+(4 x^{4} + x)(\tan^{2}{\left(x \right)} + 1) \\ & =4 x^{4} \tan^{2}{\left(x \right)} + 4 x^{4} + 16 x^{3} \tan{\left(x \right)} + 32 x^{3} + x \tan^{2}{\left(x \right)} + x + \tan{\left(x \right)} + 2\end{aligned}
$$

knowledgePoint.title: Differentiating a Product Containing an Exponential or Logarithmic Function

step.solution:
Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x) = x^2$ and $v(x)=\ln x.$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={({x}^{2})}^{′}ln⁡x+{x}^{2}{(ln⁡x)}^{′} \\  & =2x\cdot ln⁡x+{x}^{2}(\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =2xln⁡x+x \\  & =x(2ln⁡x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

step.solution:
Here, we have the product of two functions $u(x)={x}^{2}+3$ and $v(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x).$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={({x}^{2}+3)}^{′}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+({x}^{2}+3){(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x))}^{′} \\  & =(2x)(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x))+({x}^{2}+3)(\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+\frac{{x}^{2}+3}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

step.solution:
Here, we have the product of the two functions $u(x)={5}^{-x}$ and $v(x)={log}_{7}⁡(x).$ So, we apply the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x) \\  & ={({5}^{-x})}^{′}{log}_{7}⁡(x)+{5}^{-x}{({log}_{7}⁡(x))}^{′} \\  & =(-{5}^{-x}ln⁡(5))({log}_{7}⁡(x))+({5}^{-x})(\frac{1}{xln⁡(7)}) \\  & =-{5}^{-x}ln⁡(5){log}_{7}⁡(x)+\frac{{5}^{-x}}{xln⁡(7)}\end{aligned}
$$

step.markdown:
The product rule can also be written using *Leibniz notation*:

If $y = u(x) \cdot v(x),$ then 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} \cdot  v + u \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}
$$

knowledgePoint.title: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Product  at a Given Point

step.markdown: If a curve $\mathcal C$ is given by $y=e^x\sin x,$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\dfrac \pi 2.$
step.solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x) = e^x$ and $v(x)=\sin{x}.$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = e^x,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x} = \cos x.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot cos⁡x+sin⁡x\cdot {e}^{x} \\  & ={e}^{x}(cos⁡x+sin⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\dfrac\pi 2$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=\pi /2} & ={e}^{\pi /2}(cos⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+sin⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & ={e}^{\pi /2}(0+1) \\  & ={e}^{\pi /2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $e^{\pi/2}.$
step.title: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Product  at a Given Point
